Captain James Cook was an eighteenth-century British naval officer whose methodical voyages charted vast regions of the Pacific Ocean, including Australia, New Zealand, and numerous Pacific islands. He combined precise cartography, scientific observation, and relatively humane treatment of indigenous peoples, setting new standards for exploration. He began his career as a Royal Navy surveyor and gained fame for accurate charts during his participation in mapping the St. Lawrence River during the Seven Years War.

He commanded three great Pacific expeditions from 1768 to 1779 aboard the HMS Endeavour, HMS Resolution, and HMS Discovery, sponsored by the British Admiralty and the Royal Society. On his first voyage, he sailed to Tahiti to observe the transit of Venus, then charted the coasts of New Zealand and Australia, the first detailed European maps of these regions. He proved New Zealand was two islands, not a peninsula of a larger continent, and that Australia was not the fabled southern continent—fundamentally revising geographic knowledge. He discovered and named the Hawaiian Islands in his third voyage. In 1779, he was killed during a dispute with Hawaiian islanders over the theft of a ship's boat.

Beyond his discoveries, Cook instituted practices that prevented scurvy and other shipboard diseases, significantly lowering death rates on long voyages—a major contribution to maritime exploration and naval health. He brought back extensive scientific collections, botanical specimens, and detailed journals that influenced European scientific understanding of the Pacific world.
